fullName: Polarization Modulation Spectroscopy (POLAR) feature beamline at 4-ID

status2026.detail: APS Beamline Directory (entry '4-ID-B,G,H: POLAR', read 2026-10-08) lists POLAR as 'Operational/Accepting General Users' with on-site and remote access. Commissioning milestones: in Sept 2024 POLAR was expected to see first light during that run cycle (r23); in Oct 2024 it was 'nearing completion' (r24); first light came in late 2024 / early 2025 (r20). The first users arrived in the 2025-1 run (Jan–May 2025), a University of Wisconsin team studying flexomagnetism (r19). In March 2025 the beamline was still described as 'under commissioning' (r25). The APS-U project was formally completed (CD-4) after a Sept 2025 DOE review and announced in Feb 2026 (r22). As of the 2026-09-22 ID table, the source is still the two planar 3.0-cm undulators (r8). Neither the superconducting SCAPE undulators (designed for source-based polarization control over 2.7–27 keV: circular in the first harmonic, linear or elliptical with Pc ≈ 75–90% in higher harmonics) nor the permanent-magnet X-undulator alternative (1-m prototype design, minimum 2.6 keV; no upper energy stated) has been installed (r1, r4, r10, r12). Circular and vertical-linear polarization therefore still come from crystal phase retarders, which cover about 2.7–14 keV (r7, r12). By August 2025 POLAR was no longer among the five feature beamlines still awaiting first experiments (r45), and its lead engineer describes it as supporting 'experiments across three instrument stations' (r20).

tagline: Twisting X-ray light into corkscrews to reveal hidden magnetism in matter squeezed to millions of atmospheres.
plainSummary: POLAR is a 78-metre X-ray beamline at Argonne's Advanced Photon Source that controls the 'handedness' of light. X-rays from the APS normally wiggle side to side. POLAR sends them through thin, near-perfect diamond crystals that act as X-ray 'quarter-wave plates', the same kind of element that turns flat-wiggling light into twisting light in optics labs and in some 3D-cinema glasses. The crystals twist the wiggle into a left- or right-handed corkscrew, or turn it to up-and-down, and they can switch about 15 times a second. Magnetic atoms absorb left- and right-handed X-rays slightly differently, so comparing the two shows which atoms are magnetic, how strongly, and which way their tiny magnets point. Each element answers only at its own X-ray 'colour', so scientists can question iron, iridium or uranium one at a time. The upgraded APS beam is so narrow and steady that POLAR's mirrors can focus it to about 100–400 nanometres, hundreds of times thinner than a hair. That makes it possible to study specks crushed between two diamond tips to millions of atmospheres, cooled to about 1.4 degrees above absolute zero, inside a 9-tesla magnet. POLAR can also take magnetic 'X-ray photos' of domains. The goal is to discover quantum states of matter for future electronics and magnets.
expertSummary: POLAR (4-ID; stations 4-ID-B/G/H) is the APS-U feature beamline for polarization-dependent resonant spectroscopy, scattering and imaging at 2.7–27 keV. The source is two in-line planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulators (λu = 3.0 cm, 79 periods each, Keff ≈ 2.6, E1 ≈ 2.55 keV) with a phase shifter, on a windowless HHL front end. In the FOE, horizontally deflecting HHL mirrors (Si/Rh/Pt, 3 mrad, M2 bendable) feed an LN2-cooled CINEL vertical DCM. Its Si(111) crystals are joined by 6H-SiC(0006) (θB ≈ 61° at 2.8 keV). SiC is needed only for polarization generated at the source (future SCAPE/X-undulator): near 2.8 keV Si(111) sits at θB ≈ 45° and would suppress the π component. With today's phase plates, which sit after the mono, the vertical DCM sees pure σ light. An in-vacuum Bragg-transmission phase-retarder tank (C(111)/(220) diamond, thin Si(111)) delivers LCP/RCP (Pc ≈ 0.98) and L-V (Plin −0.80 to −0.95) at about 2.7–14 keV, with piezo helicity modulation near 15 Hz and lock-in detection. For focusing, horizontal toroid/cylinder mirrors at 53.7/54.5 m give 5–35 µm, an 8-stack Be transfocator gives ≥2 × 0.9 µm², and two fixed-figure KB pairs give the smallest spots. KB1 (WD 100 mm) puts 100–200 nm on a 4-ID-G Huber horizontal diffractometer, fitted with a ±2 T HTS magnet or an air-bearing imaging stack for dichroic ptychography and Bragg CDI. KB2 (WD 600 mm) puts 300–400 nm into a 4-ID-H 9-1-1 T vector magnet (1.4 K, 75 mm bore) holding a DAC with interferometry, Raman/ruby and a 7-element SDD, for XMCD/XMLD toward 6 Mbar. Calculated flux is about 1.3×10^13 ph/s at 10 keV into 114 × 92 nm² (SRI 2021 design value, 20 × 20 µrad² acceptance); the beamline directory quotes the same 1.3×10^13 ph/s. Source-based polarization switching is future scope: superconducting SCAPE devices (designed for 2.7–27 keV) or a permanent-magnet X-undulator (prototype design, from 2.6 keV).

whatAPSUEnables.plain: The old beamline at sector 4 could focus its polarized X-rays to about 15–20 micrometres. APS-U's electron beam is about 20 times narrower horizontally, so the X-ray source is smaller and its light more parallel. POLAR can now squeeze a bright polarized beam about 100 times smaller, to roughly 0.1–0.4 micrometres. At 10 keV about 200 times more of its light is also 'coherent' (laser-like). Tiny beams allow tinier samples between smaller diamond tips. The design goal is about ten times the old pressure range, roughly 6 million atmospheres, well past the ~3.6 million at Earth's centre; in 2026 the beamline lists 3 million atmospheres as available. Coherent light is meant to let scientists rebuild lens-free magnetic images of domains only tens of nanometres across; the 2026 directory quotes 400 nm for routine dichroic imaging.
whatAPSUEnables.expert: The 42 pm-rad multi-bend achromat (MBA) lattice cuts the horizontal electron beam size from about 275 to 14.5 µm and the divergence from 11 to 2.9 µrad (brightness mode). Fixed-figure KB optics can therefore demagnify to 0.1–0.4 µm even at long working distances (100 and 600 mm) chosen to fit cryostats, magnets and DACs, with about 25–40% transmission. This enables three things. (i) XANES/XMCD/XMLD in DACs with culets and samples small enough for 3–6 Mbar (double-stage or toroidal anvils), with fewer pressure-gradient and gasket artefacts. (ii) Real-space dichroic mapping at 100–400 nm and coherent dichroic imaging (ptychography/tomography, Bragg CDI) at about 10–50 nm, from a coherent fraction about 200× larger at 10 keV. (iii) Weak or diffuse resonant magnetic scattering from small crystals at pressure. On-axis swap-out injection also allows small round ID vacuum chambers. That is the precondition for the planned superconducting SCAPE sources, which would remove phase-plate losses (×5–30) and extend polarization control to 14–27 keV (actinide L edges, 4d K edges; elliptical rather than fully circular light in the higher harmonics), and for the permanent-magnet X-undulator alternative (prototype design, from 2.6 keV). These sources are not yet installed (Sept 2026).

techniques.name: X-ray magnetic circular dichroism
techniques.plain: Measure how much a material absorbs left-handed versus right-handed X-rays at an element's absorption edge. The difference is a fingerprint of that element's magnetism, telling us how strongly its atoms are magnetized and in which direction.
techniques.expert: Helicity- (or field-) modulated absorption at K edges of 3d metals, L2,3 edges of 4d metals (2.8–3.4 keV), rare-earth (4f) and 5d elements, and M4,5 edges of actinides (3.3–4 keV). 4d K edges (17–25.5 keV) and actinide L2,3 edges (16.3–22.3 keV) lie above the ~14 keV phase-plate limit and need the future polarizing source (r4, r36). Hard-x-ray XMCD amplitudes are typically 0.1–6% of the edge jump (r15), and the design goal was signals down to ~10 ppm (r4). Lock-in detection at the phase-plate modulation frequency (~13–15 Hz) is used, with a ~1–4 kHz chopper for dark-current subtraction (r12, r15). Where the L2,3 final states carry the moment (e.g. 4d and 5d metals), sum rules (Thole 1992, Carra 1993) separate orbital and spin moments (r39). At 3d K edges and rare-earth L2,3 edges the signal comes from induced 4p or 5d polarization, so the sum rules are not directly applicable and the data are interpreted more qualitatively (r15). The effect was first observed in 1987 at the Fe K edge, a hard-x-ray edge (r40).

techniques.name: X-ray (magnetic) linear dichroism
techniques.plain: Compare horizontally and vertically wiggling X-rays. This reveals lopsided electron clouds (orbitals) and antiferromagnets, where neighbouring atomic magnets cancel and show no net magnetism.
techniques.expert: L-H vs L-V absorption via a half-wave (two-plate) phase-retarder setting, with Plin ≈ −0.80 at low E and ≈ −0.95 at high E (r7). Probes orbital anisotropy, ferroelectric distortions and AFM order axes. At 4-ID-H, transverse fields up to ±1 T are available for XMLD (r12).

techniques.name: Polarized X-ray absorption near-edge / fine structure
techniques.plain: Scan the X-ray energy across an element's edge. The shape of the absorption edge shows the element's charge state (valence) and its neighbours. That shows, for example, when pressure pushes an electron out of an atom's inner f shell into the shared 'sea' of conduction electrons.
techniques.expert: Valence, mixed-valence and Kondo physics in 4f/5f systems (e.g. Yb, Eu, Ce, U) and orbital occupancy in 5d oxides under pressure, measured in transmission through the anvils or in fluorescence. Typically combined with simultaneous XMCD (r4, r12).

techniques.name: X-ray resonant magnetic scattering / diffraction
techniques.plain: Tune the X-ray energy to an element's resonance and bounce the beam off a crystal. Extra spots appear that come from the pattern of magnetic order rather than the atoms themselves.
techniques.expert: Resonant (and non-resonant) magnetic Bragg diffraction on the 4-ID-G horizontal-scattering Huber diffractometer. The detector arm is split by 25°: one branch carries a 2D PAD at 0.5–2 m, the other an APD with a full in-vacuum polarization analyzer (σ/π' separation). Sample environments include CCR (4–450 K) and He-flow cryostats, a ±2 T HTS magnet, mini-DACs (directory: 20 GPa, 2θ up to 70°, 5–325 K) and strain cells (r12, r13, r7).

techniques.name: X-ray resonant magnetic reflectivity
techniques.plain: Reflect polarized X-rays at shallow angles from thin films to map magnetism layer by layer, down to single atomic layers at interfaces.
techniques.expert: Dichroic specular and off-specular reflectivity for heterostructures. A full in-vacuum setup reaches the 4d transition-metal L edges at 2.75–3.4 keV (Ru, Rh, Pd) in fields up to 2 T (r12).

techniques.name: Dichroic ptychography and tomography
techniques.plain: Instead of using a lens, shine the coherent beam on overlapping spots and let a computer turn the speckle patterns into a magnetic image. Rotating the sample builds a 3D map of the magnetization.
techniques.expert: Coherent 100–200 nm KB beams (100 mm working distance) on a high-precision stack: ±7° double tilt, XYZ, 360° air-bearing rotation, ±15° tilt, XY and an XYZ nanopositioner with strain gauges. Planned forward-detector distances are 2.7, 4 and 10 m, with Bragg CDI at 2 m (2θ < 45°) and interferometric sample registration (r13, r12). The method follows hard-x-ray dichroic ptychography and vector nanotomography at Gd L3 (Donnelly 2016, 2017) (r31, r32). A 3D vector-tomography reconstruction pipeline is implemented at POLAR; it was demonstrated on dichroic STXM data of Nd2Fe14B pillars taken at MAX IV NanoMAX (Nd L2 edge, ~120 nm resolution), not at POLAR (r33). The beamline directory currently quotes 400 nm resolution for 'dichroic imaging' (r7).

techniques.name: Spectroscopy in the diamond anvil cell at extreme pressure, low temperature and high field
techniques.plain: A sample smaller than a grain of salt is squeezed between two diamond tips while it sits inside a superconducting magnet near absolute zero. The X-rays shine straight through the diamonds.
techniques.expert: Non-magnetic CuBe DACs with double (compression/decompression) He-gas membranes, using perforated or partially perforated anvils to cut diamond absorption at the 5–9 keV transition-metal K and rare-earth L edges (even 1 mm of diamond transmits ~10% at the Fe K edge, while partially perforated anvils leave only ~0.1–0.2 mm in the beam). Pressure is calibrated by ruby fluorescence (<100 GPa), the diamond-edge Raman shift (>100 GPa), or XRD of Au/Ag/Pt using the Holzapfel EOS (r12, r15, r28). For multi-Mbar work, double-stage or toroidal anvils are planned (r5).

scienceCases.title: Magnetism and valence of rare earths and actinides at multi-megabar pressure
scienceCases.plain: Squeezing a metal pushes its atoms together until electrons change their minds: a magnetic atom can become non-magnetic, or a material can turn into a superconductor. POLAR watches each element's electrons and magnetism as this happens.
scienceCases.expert: Pressure tunes the competition between RKKY magnetism and Kondo screening in 4f/5f lattices. Examples: Yb 4f13 (magnetic) vs 4f14 (non-magnetic) valence crossover; mixed-valence superconductivity; Pu and URu2Si2 'hidden order'. These are probed with 4f/5d L-edge XANES/XMCD at 4-ID-H at 1.4–300 K, up to 9 T and toward 6 Mbar. Actinide M4,5 edges (3.3–4 keV) and L2,3 edges (~16.3–22.3 keV) motivate the low-energy (SiC) capability and the future high-energy polarizing source (r4, r12, r5).

scienceCases.title: Hydrides and the hunt for room-temperature superconductivity
scienceCases.plain: Hydrogen-rich compounds become superconductors near room temperature, but only above a million atmospheres. Tiny, bright, polarized beams can test whether magnetism plays a role in these materials.
scienceCases.expert: Superhydrides (e.g. LaH10, Tc near 250 K at ~1.7–1.9 Mbar) and sulfides need micron-scale samples. POLAR's 0.1–0.4 µm beams and Mbar DAC instrumentation target their electronic and magnetic structure, as well as Fe-hydrides where magnetism and superconductivity interplay (r12, r5, r4).

scienceCases.title: Quantum materials under pressure: spin liquids, Mott and Kondo physics
scienceCases.plain: Pressure is a clean 'tuning knob' that changes how electrons talk to each other without adding impurities. It can push a material from insulator to metal, or freeze or melt exotic magnetic states.
scienceCases.expert: Pressure tunes bandwidth, hybridization and exchange paths in 4d/5d oxides, such as honeycomb Kitaev candidates and Sr2IrO4-type iridates (Ir L3 XMCD in a DAC was already done at 8 GPa, 11 K at 4-ID-D). It drives insulator–metal transitions in high-bulk-modulus transition-metal oxides and spin melting/freezing in frustrated magnets. Weak diffuse XRMS from short-range order demands the highest brilliance (r4, r14).

scienceCases.title: Imaging magnetic, chiral and polar (ferroelectric) textures
scienceCases.plain: Magnets and ferroelectrics break up into patterned regions (domains), swirls and 'skyrmions' that could store data. Coherent polarized X-rays can photograph them inside a crystal, not just on its surface.
scienceCases.expert: Dichroic ptychography and tomography at 10–50 nm (reciprocal space) or 100 nm (real space) target ferro/ferrimagnetic domains, skyrmion strings, AFM domains (via XMLD contrast) and polar vortices. Examples cited by the POLAR team: ferroelectric incommensurate spin crystals in SrRuO3/PbTiO3 trilayers (Rusu et al. 2022, coauthored by POLAR staff; measured at the pre-upgrade 4-ID-D, r44), and 3D magnetization in Nd2Fe14B pillars (data from MAX IV NanoMAX, reconstructed with the pipeline now implemented at POLAR) (r34, r33, r12).

scienceCases.title: Strain gradients and flexomagnetism in thin membranes (first POLAR users)
scienceCases.plain: Bending a thin crystal can make it magnetic. The first scientists to use POLAR in 2025, from the University of Wisconsin, studied this 'flexomagnetism' in thin materials for future microelectronics.
scienceCases.expert: APS reports that the first POLAR user group, from the University of Wisconsin in the 2025-1 run, studied flexomagnetism in thin materials (r19). A related UW–Madison program (Kawasaki group, arXiv Feb 2026) patterns transverse strain gradients of order 10^6 m^-1 into epitaxial GdAuGe films by helium-ion implantation (rippled GdAuGe and GdPtSb membranes are cited as related work), and lists nanoprobe XMCD among the probes needed to quantify the effect (r35). Its own nanodiffraction was done at NSLS-II HXN, not at POLAR. The Gd L3 edge (7.243 keV) is within POLAR's phase-plate range. That the POLAR users were this group is our inference.

scienceCases.title: Interfaces and heterostructures at low photon energy
scienceCases.plain: Where two thin layers meet, new magnetism can appear that neither layer has alone. POLAR measures it element by element.
scienceCases.expert: In-vacuum XMCD/XMLD/XRMR at 2.75–3.4 keV (Ru, Rh, Pd L2,3) and K edges of 3d metals in ±2 T fields on the 4-ID-G diffractometer study proximity-induced moments and spin-orbit-coupled 4d/5d layers. Uniaxial strain cells and voltage-bias cells are also supported (r12, r13).

scienceCases.title: Magnetic X-ray emission spectroscopy at extreme conditions (MagXES, in development)
scienceCases.plain: A new instrument funded in 2024 will analyse the X-rays a sample re-emits, revealing local magnetism even in materials whose magnets point every which way.
scienceCases.expert: A DOE Early Career award (2024, G. Fabbris, $550k/yr for 5 years) funds a MagXES spectrometer at POLAR for magnetism at low T, high pressure and high field, using novel spectrometer instrumentation (r21). Its status in 2026 has not been confirmed.

insertionDevices.name: APS30#4 (upstream)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator (out-of-vacuum, variable gap)
insertionDevices.notes: 79 periods (77 effective; 79 × 30 mm = 2.37 m magnetic length, computed). Device minimum gap 9.0 mm, admin minimum 9.17 mm, user minimum 9.4 mm. Keff 2.62 → E1 2.56 keV. 214 kW/mrad², 10.2 kW at 200 mA. Not a 'short' device. A reused (refurbished) pre-upgrade magnetic structure: the IPAC'24 undulator table lists the 3.0-cm period only as 'Existing IDs' (3 full-length plus 5 canted), while the new APS-U periods are 1.35, 1.4, 2.1, 2.5 and 2.8 cm; full-length devices are ~2.4 m (r9, Table 1). FDR: 'Linear 30 mm, 2 × 2.3 m at SSC' (r1).

insertionDevices.name: APS30#9 (downstream)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator (out-of-vacuum, variable gap)
insertionDevices.notes: 79 periods; device minimum gap 9.0 mm, admin minimum 9.06 mm, user minimum 9.1 mm. Keff 2.64 → E1 2.54 keV. 215 kW/mrad², 10.4 kW at 200 mA.

insertionDevices.name: In-line phase shifter (S04ID:ILPS) with corrector
insertionDevices.notes: Sets the electron path delay so that radiation from both undulators adds in phase. APS-U installed 11 phase shifters with correctors in in-line sectors (r9). Exposed in POLAR's Bluesky configuration (r26). lengthM is unknown (0 = not published).

insertionDevices.name: SCAPE (Superconducting Arbitrarily Polarizing Emitter), 2 units, NOT INSTALLED
insertionDevices.notes: Planned 'mature scope' replacement for the two planar devices. Pure circular polarization comes only in the first harmonic; higher harmonics give linear (H or V) or elliptical light with Pc tunable to ~75–90% (PDR), which is how 14–27 keV would be covered (r4). FDR: 35 mm × 1.3 m (conservative), possibly 30 mm and up to 1.8 m. PDR: 3.0 cm × 1.5 m in a single ~4.5 m cryostat. Fast switching would use ~30 µrad alternating orbit bumps at up to 10 Hz, or ~6 A undulator current bumps (r1, r4). A 0.5 m prototype (30 mm period, 16.5 periods, 10 mm magnetic gap, NbTi, 540 A operating current) was tested in 2021 (r11). The 2021 town hall planned replacement for ~2026 (r12). It requires a ~6 mm-ID round vacuum chamber. Installation is not confirmed as of Sept 2026 (r8).

insertionDevices.name: X-undulator (alternative future polarizing source), PROTOTYPE STAGE
insertionDevices.type: fixed-gap APPLE-X-like pure permanent-magnet undulator with force-compensation arrays
insertionDevices.polarization: all states (circular, elliptical, linear at any angle)
insertionDevices.notes: Four NdFeB Halbach arrays around an 8.5 mm bore (6.0/7.5 mm ID/OD round chamber); max Keff 2.6 → 2.6 keV minimum. K and polarization are set by longitudinal array motion. Switching takes 1 Hz via quarter-period shift, or ~5 Hz with a dual-XU detuning scheme. 1-m prototype design (IPAC'24) (r10). Funded by a 2023 LDRD 'Force-neutral fast polarization switching X-undulator for the POLAR beamline' (r30). Not installed.

source.canting: None. The two planar undulators are in line (collinear) in the 4-ID straight, separated by a phase shifter (r2, r8). Before the upgrade, sector 4 was canted, with a circularly polarizing electromagnetic undulator (CPU, 12.8 cm period) feeding soft-x-ray 4-ID-C and, in 2002, Undulator A (3.3 cm) feeding hard-x-ray 4-ID-D (r29); by 2018 the 4-ID-D source was a 2.4 m, 3.5 cm-period SmCo undulator (r16). APS-U gave the whole straight to POLAR's hard-x-ray line (r18).
source.frontEnd: Standard APS-U High-Heat-Load front end, windowless with differential pumping, rated 21 kW total and 590 kW/mrad² peak (r2, r1). The design is based on the 28-ID HHLFE. Elements in order: LPPS, storage-ring valve, burn-through fixed mask BTFM1, fixed mask FM2, collimator, GRID XBPM, FM3, photon shutter PS2 with intensity monitor, redundant safety shutters SS1/SS2, wall collimator, front-end valve, exit mask with XBPM2, exit collimator, beamline isolation valve (r2). Exit mask aperture is 2 × 2 mm (H × V) at ~25.4 m and the exit collimator is 5 × 5 mm at ~26.1 m (r1). Total power when the undulator is tuned to 2.8 keV (linear) is ~16 kW, with ~512 W/mm² on the white-beam slits at 27 m (r1).
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at the ID source point, from the FDR Table 1.1 design (r3). Brightness mode (324 bunches, 42 pm): σx = 14.7 µm, σx' = 2.8 µrad, σy = 3.2 µm, σy' = 1.3 µrad. Timing mode (48 bunches, 32 pm effective): σx = 12.9 µm, σx' = 2.5 µrad, σy = 8.8 µm, σy' = 3.7 µrad. The 2021 town hall quotes σx = 14.5 µm and σx' = 2.9 µrad, vs 275 µm and 11 µrad for the old APS (r12). The single-electron photon terms at 10 keV for L ≈ 2.4 m are σr ≈ √(2λL)/4π ≈ 2 µm and σr' ≈ √(λ/2L) ≈ 5 µrad (computed here, approximate). The two undulators sit about ±1.3 m from the straight-section center, so focusing optics see two longitudinally separated sources. PDR ray tracing for ±1 m sources showed slightly asymmetric KB spots, mitigated with defining slits (r4).

branches.name: 4-ID-B: toroid optics + 2 T electromagnet XMCD station
branches.description: The upstream experimental enclosure. It holds the horizontal toroid/cylinder focusing mirrors (53.7 and 54.5 m) that serve 4-ID-G and 4-ID-H, beam conditioning (diamond window, in-line polarimeter, diamond XBPM, chopper, attenuators) and an existing water-cooled 2 T electromagnet with bendable 'KB3' mirrors. That station does fast-field-switching XMCD on bulk, film and low-pressure samples (r12, r5, r26). It sits on the same straight line as G and H, and beam for G/H passes through B.

branches.name: 4-ID-G: diffraction, reflectivity & dichroic imaging (new enclosure)
branches.description: A new enclosure built during the APS-U dark period (planned for Sept–Dec 2023). Transfocator (CRLs) 2 m upstream of the sample, KB1 (100 mm working distance) and a Huber horizontal-scattering diffractometer at ~67.2 m. The diffractometer carries either an open Eulerian cradle with a ±2 T HTS magnet or a high-precision imaging stack for ptychography and Bragg CDI (r12, r13, r5).

branches.name: 4-ID-H: extreme-conditions spectroscopy (new enclosure)
branches.description: The last enclosure, also new. KB2 (600 mm working distance) focuses into the 9-1-1 T vector magnet at ~73.3 m, which holds a DAC with nanopositioners, interferometers, a Raman/ruby system and a fluorescence detector, for XMCD/XMLD to multi-Mbar. An existing 4 T cryogen-free magnet sits downstream (beam-pass mode), followed by the beam stop (r12, r13, r1). G and H operate alternately; H can be prepared and its magnet cooled while G takes beam (r5).

components.name: Upstream undulator APS30#4
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Center of the upstream device: two ~2.4 m devices plus a phase shifter share the ~5 m straight. Inferred, no published coordinate.
components.plain: A 2.4-metre row of alternating magnets that makes the electrons slalom 79 times, so they shine a bright, horizontally polarized X-ray beam.
components.expert: Planar hybrid PM, λu = 3.0 cm, N = 79, device minimum gap 9.0 mm (user 9.4 mm), Keff = 2.62, E1 = 2.56 keV at 6 GeV. 214 kW/mrad² and 10.2 kW at 200 mA. Higher odd harmonics reach 27 keV.

components.name: In-line phase shifter + corrector
components.distanceNote: Approximate: between the two undulators near the straight-section center (inferred)
components.plain: A small magnetic 'detour' that makes the electrons arrive at the second undulator exactly in step, so the light from both undulators adds up.
components.expert: Gap-adjustable phase shifter (EPICS S04ID:ILPS), set as a function of undulator gap for in-phase radiation. Corrector magnets correct the orbit. APS-U installed 11 such units in in-line sectors.

specs.purpose: constructive interference of the two undulators

components.name: Downstream undulator APS30#9
components.distanceNote: Approximate center of the downstream device (inferred)
components.plain: The second undulator, in line with the first, which roughly doubles the flux.
components.expert: Planar hybrid PM, λu = 3.0 cm, N = 79, device minimum gap 9.0 mm (user 9.1 mm), Keff = 2.64, E1 = 2.54 keV. 215 kW/mrad² and 10.4 kW at 200 mA. A future SCAPE or X-undulator pair would replace both devices (not installed as of Sept 2026).

components.name: High-heat-load front end (windowless)
components.distanceNote: Schematic placeholder. The front end spans from the ring (~13 m) to inside the FOE (~26 m); individual element positions are not published. The ratchet (shield) wall is at ~23.7–24.4 m on the 2021 plan (r12).
components.plain: The safety gateway between the accelerator and the beamline. Thick metal masks and shutters can stop up to 21 kilowatts of X-ray power and block stray radiation.
components.expert: APS-U HHLFE (based on the 28-ID design): LPPS, SRV, burn-through fixed mask BTFM1, FM2, collimator, GRID XBPM1, FM3, PS2/IM1, safety shutters SS1/SS2, wall collimator, FEV, exit mask/XBPM2, exit collimator, BIV. Limits 21 kW and 590 kW/mrad². Differentially pumped, no Be window, preserving coherence and low-energy flux.

components.name: Front-end exit mask (with XBPM2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16
components.plain: A water-cooled copper block with a 2 mm square hole that lets only the useful central X-ray beam through.
components.expert: Standard HHL front-end exit mask, 2 × 2 mm (H × V) aperture, with XBPM2 at the last front-end table inside the FOE.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16
components.plain: A heavy-metal block that stops high-energy 'bremsstrahlung' radiation produced by the electron beam.
components.expert: Exit collimator narrowed to a 5 × 5 mm aperture to help beamlines manage bremsstrahlung with small-offset monochromators.

components.name: High-heat-load white-beam slits (4ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16. The 2021 plan shows the slit at ~26.8–27.6 m (scaled).
components.plain: Adjustable tungsten jaws that trim the raw beam to the bright central cone, cutting the heat that reaches the optics.
components.expert: HHL white-beam slits with tungsten edge inserts. A typical 0.5 × 0.5 mm² opening at 25–27 m accepts ~20 × 20 µrad², used for all flux and spot calculations. 0.92 × 0.92 mm² accepts the full cone at 2.8 keV. Incident power density ~512 W/mm² when tuned to 2.8 keV. Bluesky motors: horizontal, diagonal, pitch, yaw. The FDR gives 432 W through a 0.92 × 0.92 mm² opening with the undulators tuned to 2.8 keV, i.e. the slits throw away ~97% of the ~16 kW total.

specs.maxPowerThroughSlit: 432 W (0.92 × 0.92 mm² at 27 m, undulators tuned to 2.8 keV; FDR Table 4.15)

components.name: White-beam mirror pair M1 (flat) + M2 (bendable)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 (dual mirror system in one vessel). The 2021 plan shows the tank at ~27.6–29.2 m (scaled).
components.plain: Two super-polished silicon mirrors, hit at a grazing angle of 0.17°, that soak up most of the heat and filter out unwanted high-energy X-rays before the crystals.
components.expert: Water-cooled single-crystal Si, 320 mm long (300 mm active), 3 mrad horizontal deflection each, double bounce with ~4 mm lateral offset. Stripes Pt/Rh/bare Si (5 mm wide each) for harmonic rejection. M1 is flat with a notch to reduce thermal deformation. M2 is meridionally bendable (R = ±50 km) to cancel the M1 and DCM-crystal heat bumps. Slope error <0.1 µrad, roughness <0.2 nm. Absorbed power 254 W (M1) and 118 W (M2) at 2.8 keV.

components.name: Photon mask / pink-beam stop (4ID-PM-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16
components.plain: A cooled block that catches any unreflected white beam so that only mirror-filtered light continues.
components.expert: Photon mask / pink-beam stop between the HHL mirrors and the DCM.

components.name: Beam-viewing flags and cameras (4-ID-A: after the mirrors and after the mono)
components.distanceNote: Approximate; shown at the post-mirror flag. The Bluesky configuration defines two 4-ID-A flag cameras, PostMirrBeam (between the mirror tank at 28.5 m and the DCM at 30.0 m, so ~29.6 m) and PostMonoBeam (after the DCM, ~31 m). Positions are not published.
components.plain: Retractable fluorescent screens watched by cameras, so staff can see where the beam is after the mirrors and after the monochromator.
components.expert: Two retractable YAG/fluorescent flags with Vimba cameras: 4idaPostMirrBeam (after the HHL mirrors) and 4idaPostMonoBeam (after the VDCM); used for alignment and for checking stripe and crystal changes (r26).

components.name: Vertical double-crystal monochromator (CINEL), Si(111) + 6H-SiC(0006)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 (30.0 m, then specified as a horizontal DCM). The 2021 plan drawing shows the DCM at ~30.2–31.1 m (scaled). As built it is vertical-deflecting (r5, r26).
components.plain: Two perfect crystals act like a prism for X-rays and pick out a single 'colour' (energy) with 0.01% precision. Turning them scans the energy across an element's absorption edge.
components.expert: LN2-cooled, side-cooled crystals. Si(111) (d = 3.135 Å) covers 2.75–27 keV. 6H-SiC(0006) (d = 2.522 Å, θB = 61.4° at 2.8 keV) is used at 2.75–3.2 keV: Si(111) is at θB ≈ 45° near 2.8 keV and would suppress π (vertical) polarization in vertical diffraction. The large first crystal has only a Bragg rotation (the beam walks on it). The small second crystal has coarse and piezo pitch/roll for XBPM feedback in B, G and H. Fixed exit with 15.6 mm offset. Stability spec 50 nrad RMS. ΔE/E ≈ 1.4×10^-4. Changed from the FDR's horizontal DCM: the vertical geometry keeps the source's linear-H light σ-polarized at all angles. SiC matters only once polarization is generated at the source; with the phase plates downstream of the mono, Si(111) at 2.8 keV still reflects the σ (linear-H) beam (r4, r12). The Bluesky mono device has a crystal-select motor (r26); whether the SiC pair is installed and in use in 2026 is not published.

components.name: Monochromatic-beam slits (4ID-SL-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16
components.plain: Jaws that clean up the edges of the monochromatic beam.
components.expert: In-vacuum JJ-type four-blade slits (Bluesky 'monoslt', 4idVDCM motors m13–m16).

components.name: Secondary/bremsstrahlung collimators and white-beam stop
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16: secondary collimator 31.3 m, photon mask/WB stop 31.7 m, primary bremsstrahlung collimator 32.0 m
components.plain: Shielding blocks that make sure only the offset monochromatic beam leaves the first hutch.
components.expert: 4ID-SC-1 (31.3 m), 4ID-PM-2 WB stop (31.7 m), 4ID-BC-1 (32.0 m). The vertical mono offset lets the stop intercept the undeflected white and bremsstrahlung line.

components.name: In-vacuum phase-retarder tank (diamond and Si phase plates)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16. The 2021 plan shows the tank at ~33.0–33.9 m (scaled). This is the existing 4-ID-D tank, reused.
components.plain: The heart of POLAR. A thin, near-perfect diamond is tilted a hair's breadth off its reflecting angle and acts as a 'quarter-wave plate', turning flat-wiggling X-rays into left- or right-handed corkscrews. Wiggling the diamond with a piezo flips the twist about 15 times a second.
components.expert: Bragg-transmission phase retarders. Plates pr1 and pr2 are diamond with selectable C(111) (d = 2.0595 Å) or C(220) (d = 1.261 Å) reflections; pr3 is Si(111). The diffraction plane is set at 45° to the linear-H polarization so σ and π are equal. Near the Bragg angle the σ and π waves propagate with different phase velocities: δ ≈ (π/2)·Δθq/Δθ. One quarter-wave plate gives LCP/RCP (sign of Δθ). Two plates in tandem give δ = π, i.e. linear-V. Piezo (PI E-665) AC offset modulation drives lock-in XMCD. The 4-ID-D legacy set used 50–500 µm diamonds for 3.2–15 keV and a 10 µm Si(111) plate for 2.8–3.2 keV. Costs: ×5–30 flux loss, 5–30% LCP/RCP intensity asymmetry, and impractical above ~14 keV. Principle: Hirano, Ishikawa & Kikuta (r41). The Bragg-transmission diamond plates used at APS sector 4 were developed by Lang & Srajer (r38).

specs.plates: pr1, pr2: C(111)/C(220) diamond; pr3: Si(111)

components.name: Monochromatic station shutter (4ID-SH-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16; the 2021 plan shows it at ~34.2–35.5 m
components.plain: A heavy safety shutter that lets the beam out of the first hutch only when the downstream hutch is searched and closed.
components.expert: Station beam shutter (PSS 'SBS') controlling beam into 4-ID-B (PV PA:04ID:B_BEAM_PRESENT).

components.name: Shielded beam transport, 4-ID-A → 4-ID-B
components.distanceNote: Spans ~36.1–50.5 m (2021 plan, scaled); midpoint given
components.plain: A 14-metre lead-shielded vacuum pipe carries the beam across the experiment hall floor to the experimental hutches.
components.expert: Existing shielded transport pipe on stands every few metres (2021 plan), then the small legacy mini-hutch 4-ID-MH (~50.5–52.8 m). (An earlier draft called it 'U1-40'; that label could not be found on the published drawings.)

components.name: 4-ID-B entrance slits (bslt)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. The FDR places a mono slit (SL-3) just upstream of the toroids (47.3 m in the FDR layout); the as-built toroids are at 53.7 m. Position inferred.
components.plain: Jaws that set how much beam reaches the focusing mirrors.
components.expert: JJ slits (4idbSoft m10–m13). Order follows FDR Table 4.16; position scaled to the 2021 layout.

components.name: Toroidal focusing mirror M3 (bendable)
components.distanceNote: 2021 town hall slide 'Reflectivities/cut-offs' (toroidal double mirrors at 53.7 and 54.5 m)
components.plain: A curved, metal-coated mirror that gently focuses the whole beam to a spot a few tens of micrometres wide, for experiments that need lots of photons rather than a tiny spot.
components.expert: Horizontal-deflecting, 2–4 mrad, 540 mm (520 active), meridional bender 4–100 km. Stripes (SRI 2021): Pd sagittal cylinder plus flats of bare Si and Pt. FDR 2019 had Si (R_s 83.1 mm) and Pt (79 mm) cylinders plus a Pd flat. Focus at 67.2 m (G) or 73.3 m (H). Also suppresses harmonics. Retracted for KB/CRL modes. Slope error 0.2–0.3 µrad.

components.name: Cylinder/flat mirror M4
components.distanceNote: 2021 town hall slide (53.7 and 54.5 m)
components.plain: A second mirror that sends the beam back parallel to its original path and completes the focusing and filtering.
components.expert: Horizontal-deflecting, 2–4 mrad, 540 mm, R_m > 100 km, 40 mm thick. Stripes (SRI 2021): Pd flat plus Si and Pt sagittal cylinders (FDR: Si flat, Pd cylinder R_s 69.9 mm, Pt flat). Double bounce with M3, so the beam exits parallel with a few-mm lateral offset (~0.8 m × 2θ, computed). Together with M1/M2 it gives harmonic rejection across 2.7–27 keV.

components.name: Beam-viewing flag after the toroidal mirrors (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: just downstream of M4 (54.5 m); inferred from the device name only.
components.plain: A screen and camera that show the beam after the focusing mirrors, so they can be steered.
components.expert: Vimba flag camera 4idbPostToroBeam, used to align the M3/M4 toroid/cylinder pair (r26).

components.name: Diamond vacuum window
components.distanceNote: Approximate. A small component on the 2021 plan ~0.8 m after M4 (the FDR window was 0.8 m after M4). The FDR specified 'Be or diamond'; Bluesky confirms a diamond window with x/y stages in 4-ID-B.
components.plain: A thin diamond sheet that seals the ultra-clean vacuum of the optics from the experiment section while letting X-rays pass almost untouched.
components.expert: Separates the windowless UHV optics section (front end → toroids) from the end-station vacuum. Diamond (rather than Be) helps preserve coherence. On motorized x/y stages (4idbSoft m1/m2).

components.name: In-line X-ray polarimeter
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Placed on the 4-ID-B optics table (~57.5–60 m on the 2021 plan) following the FDR component order; the FDR position (53.4 m) predates the toroid move.
components.plain: A 'polarization meter'. A foil scatters a little of the beam sideways to two detectors at right angles. Turning the device around the beam measures how the light is polarized.
components.expert: Retractable scattering foil at 45° to the beam, two detectors 90° apart (horizontal and vertical preamps), rotatable about the beam axis for in-line polarization determination. PDR described it as a 90° scatterer, collimator and two photodiodes rotating azimuthally in unison.

components.name: Diamond XBPM / TetrAMM (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (FDR order, scaled to the 2021 plan)
components.plain: A transparent diamond sensor that tells the computer where the beam is, so it can nudge the monochromator crystal and keep the beam locked in place.
components.expert: In-vacuum retractable diamond XBPM read by a TetrAMM. It is the feedback source ('Feedback B') for second-crystal pitch/roll PZTs, with a 0.1 µrad stability goal. The public 4-ID status page lists separate position-feedback loops for stations B, G and H (r42).

components.name: In-vacuum optical chopper
components.distanceNote: Approximate (FDR order, scaled)
components.plain: A spinning slotted wheel that blinks the beam on and off thousands of times a second, so the detectors can subtract their own electronic noise.
components.expert: UHV-compatible chopper (design heritage: XTIP SX-STM chopper, Chang et al. 2016), up to 4 kHz, on a translation stage. Used for double-lock-in detection: dark current at the chopper frequency, dichroism at the helicity frequency.

components.name: Attenuators / filters (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (FDR order, scaled)
components.plain: Metal foils that can be slid in to dim the beam.
components.expert: APS filter box (4idbSoft:filter).

components.name: Bendable KB mirrors 'KB3' for the 2 T electromagnet
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Inferred from the 2021 plan table position upstream of the electromagnet; FDR: 55.1 m relative to the magnet at 55.8 m.
components.plain: A pair of adjustable-curvature mirrors (one bends vertically, one horizontally) that focus the beam onto samples in the electromagnet.
components.expert: Existing bendable KB (FDR 4ID-MR-3). The PDR noted the bender exists with new 200 mm mirrors and WD ~0.4 m. The legacy 4-ID-D Rh-coated KB was 10 cm (V) / 20 cm (H) and gave ~15 × 15 µm with the toroid. Labeled 'KB3' in the 2023 workshop optics schematic. PDR 2017: 'tunable x-ray spot size down to ~10 µm' (r4).

specs.focus: down to ~10 µm (PDR 2017 design value; as-built value not published)

components.name: Incident-intensity monitor I0 (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (FDR order, scaled)
components.plain: Counts how many X-rays hit the sample, so absorption can be measured as a ratio.
components.expert: Ion chamber/photodiode I0 with SR570-type preamp (4idbSoft:A3).

components.name: 2 T electromagnet XMCD station (existing)
components.distanceNote: Approximate, measured from the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan (scale ±0.3 m). FDR: 55.8 m in its earlier layout.
components.plain: A water-cooled electromagnet whose field can be flipped in seconds, so dichroism can be measured quickly on films, crystals and samples under modest pressure, without liquid helium.
components.expert: Existing 4-ID-D electromagnet (Kepco BOP supply) with flow cryostat and ruby system. The PDR quotes P < 1 Mbar, T > 10 K and H ≈ 0.8 T across a DAC-sized pole gap, with 2 T maximum at small gaps. It allows fast field ramping and switching for field-dependent XMCD. Sample and magnet x/y/rotation stages. Evidence that it is active: the Bluesky configuration loads the 4-ID-B electromagnet, its KB mirrors and a Kepco magnet driver (r26), and POLAR's lead engineer describes 'three instrument stations' (r20). It is not listed as an end station in the beamline directory (r7), so its user-program status is unconfirmed.

specs.field: up to 2 T (≈0.8 T with DAC gap)

components.name: Transmission photodiode I (4-ID-B)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (2021 plan feature just downstream of the magnet)
components.plain: Measures how many X-rays made it through the sample.
components.expert: Photodiode with preamp (4idbSoft:A4) for transmission XAS/XMCD.

components.name: Diamond XBPM (Sydor) + slits/filters at 4-ID-G entrance
components.distanceNote: Approximate (start of the 4-ID-G optics table, ~64.1 m on the 2021 plan)
components.plain: Beam-position sensor and beam-shaping jaws in front of the focusing optics.
components.expert: Sydor diamond BPM (4idgSydor T4U) and XBPM for 'Feedback G'. Includes an AVS-type filter box (4idPyFilter) and JJ slits (gslt).

components.name: Transfocator (Be compound refractive lenses)
components.distanceNote: 2 m upstream of the diffractometer (r12). The 2021 plan shows the CRL at ~65.25 m.
components.plain: A stack of tiny curved beryllium lenses. Like adding glasses, sliding more lenses in makes the focus stronger, giving a micrometre-sized spot.
components.expert: 8 stacks of 2D parabolic Be lenses. N = 1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 8, 16 with R = 1000, 500, 200, 200, 200, 200, 100, 100 µm (FDR had 7 stacks). Binary combinations are chosen by the PyCRL controller for energy and focal size, tracking energy (chromatic). Translation along the beam. Spot ≥2 × 0.9 µm², 1.4×10^13 cps at 10 keV, usable 3–20 keV.

components.name: KB1: fixed-figure nano-focusing KB mirrors (100 mm working distance)
components.distanceNote: Approximate. Computed from the sample at 67.2 m minus the 100 mm working distance and half-lengths of the FDR KB1 mirrors (VFM 275 mm upstream of HFM 115 mm).
components.plain: Two tiny curved mirrors, one focusing up-down and one side-to-side, squeeze the beam to about 100 nanometres right in front of the sample.
components.expert: Prefigured elliptical-cylinder Si mirrors at 3 mrad, Pt and Rh stripes (5 mm each). FDR KB1: VFM 275 mm (q = 362.5 mm), HFM 115 mm (q = 157.5 mm), figure error <2 nm PV (<0.5 nm RMS), roughness 0.15 nm. Piezo, picomotor and capacitive-sensor motions. Spot 114 × 92 nm² and 1.3×10^13 ph/s at 10 keV; with a slit, coherent mode gives 200 × 200 nm² and 1.6×10^12 ph/s.

components.name: Huber horizontal-scattering diffractometer (6-circle 'APS POLAR' geometry)
components.distanceNote: Sample position: toroid focus point 67.2 m (r12) matches the 2021 plan (~67.3 m). FDR 2019 had the diffractometer at 61.3 m in a different hutch arrangement.
components.plain: A precision robot arm-and-turntable that holds the sample and a detector. It finds the angles where X-rays bounce off magnetic patterns in a crystal.
components.expert: Horizontal-scattering design. The vertical sample circle is omitted, leaving room for sample environments. Circles: τ (whole), μ (θ in the horizontal plane), χ, φ, γ, δ (hklpy 'ApsPolar' geometry), with full 360° azimuth about the cryostat axis. Option 1: open Eulerian cradle, ±29.75° χ-opening, χ ±100°. Option 2: high-precision imaging stack. The split detector arm (25° offset) carries a 2D PAD at 0.5–2 m and an APD with in-vacuum polarization analyzer. Detector rail and filters on the arm.

specs.geometry: 4S+2D horizontal (τ, μ, χ, φ, γ, δ)

components.name: ±2 T HTS split-pair magnet (diffractometer)
components.distanceNote: Mounted on the diffractometer at the sample position
components.plain: A compact superconducting magnet, cooled by a refrigerator rather than liquid helium, that can point its 2-tesla field along the beam or across it.
components.expert: Custom high-Tc superconducting magnet, Cryomech AL63 GM cooler (orientation-insensitive), 60.4 mm pole gap, warm bore with full vacuum capability. Field actively controlled (no persistent mode); 0→2 T in 5 min (−2→2 T in 7.5 min); homogeneity <0.07% over 10 mm DSV. Axial opening ±6°; radial opening 190° × 45° (100 mm height). Accepts cryostats, mini-DACs and strain cells, with field ∥ beam (spectroscopy) or ⊥ beam (diffraction). The public 4-ID status page labels it '2T Magnet (HTS-110)', i.e. presumably built by HTS-110 Ltd (r42).

components.name: High-precision goniometer for dichroic ptychography / Bragg CDI
components.distanceNote: Replaces the Eulerian cradle on the diffractometer base
components.plain: An ultra-steady sample stage that can scan and spin a sample with nanometre precision, so a computer can build 2D and 3D magnetic images from the scattered light.
components.expert: Stack, bottom to top: double tilt (±7°), XYZ translation, air-bearing rotation (360°), tilt (±15°), XY translation, XYZ nanopositioner with strain gauges. Interferometry registers beam and sample position. Uses for 2D/3D dichroic ptychography, real-space dichroic imaging/tomography (small electromagnet) and dichroic Bragg CDI. The Bluesky configuration also has a Kepco-driven magnet device for 4-ID-G, probably the 'small electromagnet' used for real-space dichroic imaging (inference, r26, r13).

components.name: Vortex ME-4 silicon drift detector (fluorescence)
components.distanceNote: Near the sample
components.plain: Measures the characteristic X-ray 'glow' of each element in the sample.
components.expert: Energy-resolving 4-element SDD for fluorescence-yield XMCD/XAS and resonant-scattering background suppression.

components.name: In-vacuum polarization analyzer + APD (detector arm)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (~1 m from the sample on the point-detector branch of the split arm; not published)
components.plain: A second crystal set at a 90° scattering angle that passes only one polarization of the scattered X-rays, proving whether a signal is magnetic.
components.expert: Full in-vacuum analyzer with motions 2θ ±11°, η −110/+30°, χ ±5°. The analyzer crystal is chosen per edge to reach 2θ_A ≈ 90° and separate σ' and π'; the Bluesky analyzer list includes PG(001), Cu, Au, Al, Si, Ge, LiF, MgO, Mo, Pd and Pt reflections (r26, analyzerlist.dat; a calculation list, not an inventory). Detection by avalanche photodiode (APD).

specs.analyzerCrystals: PG(001), Cu, Au, Al, Si, Ge, LiF, MgO, Mo, Pd, Pt …

components.name: Eiger2 X 1M pixel-array detector (also Lambda 750k)
components.distanceNote: Variable 0.5–2 m from the sample on the PAD branch; 1.5 m shown. For forward ptychography, detector distances of 2.7, 4 and 10 m are planned; 10 m would reach into 4-ID-H, unconfirmed.
components.plain: A fast X-ray 'camera' that records diffraction spots and the speckle patterns used to rebuild images.
components.expert: Dectris Eiger2 X 1M (2023 slides) on a rail, plus a Lambda 750k. Used for resonant diffraction, CDI and ptychography. The 'X-ray eye' camera is on the Huber detector arm.

components.name: Beam stop / shutter at the 4-ID-G → 4-ID-H wall (inferred)
components.distanceNote: Inferred. The 2021 elevation drawing shows an unlabelled box on the beam at ~69.6–69.9 m, just upstream of the G/H wall. Identity and as-built status are not published.
components.plain: Something must stop the beam at the end of 4-ID-G so people can work in 4-ID-H while 4-ID-G runs; this block probably does that job.
components.expert: SRI 2021 states that 4-ID-H can be accessed for preparation, magnet cooling and maintenance while 4-ID-G takes beam, which requires a radiation-safety beam stop or shutter at the G/H boundary; the public status page lists enclosure and shutter states for A, B, G and H (r5, r42). The FDR had an equivalent 'Shutter, Mono, 4ID-SH-2' at the end of its diffractometer hutch (r1). Treat as unconfirmed.

components.name: Diamond XBPM (Sydor) at 4-ID-H entrance
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16. The magnet position (73.3 m) is unchanged between FDR and as-built, so the upstream H positions are kept.
components.plain: Keeps the beam locked on the tiny sample in the big magnet.
components.expert: Diamond XBPM (4ID-BD-2; 4idhSydor) and XBPM for 'Feedback H' to the mono second-crystal PZTs.

components.name: Slits (4-ID-H)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16 (4ID-SL-6, existing)
components.plain: Jaws that define how much of the KB mirrors is lit.
components.expert: JJ slits (hslt). Limiting KB illumination also removes spot asymmetry from the two longitudinally displaced undulator sources (PDR ray tracing).

components.name: Attenuators (4-ID-H)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.16
components.plain: Foils to dim the beam.
components.expert: 4ID-FL-1.

components.name: KB2: long-working-distance KB mirrors (600 mm WD)

geometryNotes: One straight, non-canted line from the 4-ID straight, with two collinear planar undulators separated by a phase shifter. Before the upgrade, sector 4 was canted, feeding soft-x-ray 4-ID-C (CPU undulator) and 4-ID-E/XTIP plus hard-x-ray 4-ID-D. Those branches are gone, and POLAR uses the whole straight (r18, r12, r29). Beam offsets along the line, all small for a 3D model: (1) The HHL mirror pair deflects horizontally at 3 mrad each and returns the beam parallel with ~4 mm lateral offset; the direction (inboard/outboard) is not published. (2) The vertical DCM has a fixed 15.6 mm vertical offset, assumed upward. (3) The phase plates transmit the beam straight through, with each plate's diffraction plane tilted 45° about the beam. (4) The M3/M4 toroid/cylinder pair (53.7/54.5 m) deflects horizontally at 2–4 mrad each and returns the beam parallel with a few-mm offset. The pair retracts for KB/CRL modes, so the downstream beam axis differs slightly between toroid and KB modes. (5) Each KB pair has the VFM upstream of the HFM, at 3 mrad each. Enclosures (scaled from the 2021 'Sector 4 2024' plan, ±0.3 m): 4-ID-A 24.4–36.1 m (inside the hall, against the ratchet wall); shielded transport 36.1–50.5 m; mini-hutch 4-ID-MH 50.5–52.8 m; 4-ID-B 52.8–63.3 m (~2.5 m wide, existing, tapered at its downstream end); 4-ID-G 63.5–70.0 m and 4-ID-H 70.0–77.7 m (both new, ~4.6 m wide, H's outboard wall angled inward at the downstream end). All are on the experiment-hall floor (no long-beamline building). The control room sits on the outboard side alongside B/G, next to the existing XTIP rooms. Outboard double doors on B, G and H; an extra double door at H's downstream inboard corner; a staircase and loading platform beside the 9-1-1 magnet; the 9-1-1 magnet translates inboard for beam-pass. The neighbouring 5-BM hutches lie on the inboard side. Note the hutch-name churn: in the PDR (2017) the instruments were in 4-ID-B and 4-ID-D; in the FDR (2019) the SOE was 4-ID-E and the instruments were in 4-ID-B (diffractometer at 61.3 m) and 4-ID-G (magnet at 73.3 m); as built (2021 design onward) the diffractometer is in new 4-ID-G at ~67.2 m and the magnet in new 4-ID-H at 73.3 m (r1, r4, r12). Schematic hints for the unpublished offset directions: the 2021 town-hall layout cartoon (slide 16) draws the DCM with the beam stepping up between the crystals (upward offset) and the M1/M2 pair stepping the beam toward the ring (inboard). It is a cartoon, not an engineering drawing. Hutch heights scaled from the 2021 elevation (slide 16): 4-ID-A and 4-ID-B ≈ 3.4 m, 4-ID-MH ≈ 2.0 m, 4-ID-G ≈ 4.2 m, 4-ID-H ≈ 6.2 m; beam height ≈ 1.4 m above the floor (all ±0.3 m).

interactiveIdeas.title: Make it twist: the diamond quarter-wave plate
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors turn a dial that tilts a virtual diamond plate a few tens of arcseconds off its Bragg angle. Two arrows (σ and π components, set at 45°) slip out of step, and the output field traces a line, then an ellipse, then a circle; crossing zero offset reverses the handedness. A 'flip' button wiggles the piezo at 15 Hz and the corkscrew alternates. An energy slider shows the needed offset shrinking at higher energy, until above ~14 keV the plate stops working well.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How a perfect crystal changes linear into circular polarization, why helicity can be flipped mechanically, and why POLAR wants a polarizing undulator for 14–27 keV.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Bragg-transmission phase retarder: δ(Δθ) = (π/2)·Δθq/Δθ, with quarter-wave offset Δθq = 2·t·cosθB·r_e²·λ³·Re(F_h·F_h̄)/(π²·V²) (form used in APS-4ID-POLAR's Pharet calculator, r27). Example computed here: C(111), t = 500 µm, 10 keV (θB = 17.5°, |F|² = 32 f², f_C ≈ 3.0, V = 45.4 Å³) gives Δθq ≈ 2×10^-4 rad ≈ 42″. Pc = sin δ; ±Δθ gives opposite helicity. Two plates (δ = π) give linear-V. The degree of circular polarization degrades when angular divergence and the mono bandwidth (ΔE/E ≈ 1.4×10^-4 maps to Δθ = tanθB·ΔE/E) are not ≪ Δθ. Transmission falls by ×5–30 over 2.8–14 keV, and LCP/RCP intensities differ by 5–30% (r14, r4). The plate's scattering plane must be at 45° to the incident polarization.

interactiveIdeas.title: The magnetic handshake: XMCD at an absorption edge
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors pick an element (Fe K, Gd L3, Ir L3, U M5) and a magnetized sample. Two absorption curves for left and right helicity appear; their difference reveals the magnet. Flipping the magnetic field (or helicity) inverts the difference. A noise slider shows why 15 Hz switching with lock-in detection beats slow scans.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Element-specific magnetism, why the energy must be tuned to an edge, and how scientists dig sub-percent signals out of noise.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: μ± = μ0·(1 ± Pc·cosφ·A(E)), where φ is the angle between helicity and magnetization. Hard-x-ray XMCD amplitudes are 0.1–6% of the edge jump (r15); POLAR's design goal was down to ~10 ppm (r4). Sum rules at L2,3: m_orb ∝ ∫(ΔμL3 + ΔμL2), m_spin + 7⟨T_z⟩ ∝ ∫ΔμL3 − 2∫ΔμL2 (r39). Artefact check: a 0.1 µrad beam-angle change at 8 keV shifts Si(111) energy by ~3 meV (r4), so the polarization should be switched at every energy point. Real edge energies: Fe K 7.112, Gd L3 7.243, Ir L3 11.215, U M5 3.552 keV (r36).

interactiveIdeas.title: Squeeze it: beam size vs pressure in a diamond anvil cell
interactiveIdeas.concept: A two-diamond press with a culet-size slider. As the visitor shrinks the tips, the pressure gauge climbs (100 GPa = 1 Mbar ≈ 0.6 eV/Å³, since 1 eV/Å³ ≈ 160 GPa; ~3.6 Mbar at Earth's centre), but the sample shrinks too. Overlaid beams compare the old ~15 µm spot, which spills onto the metal gasket, with POLAR's 0.3 µm spot, which fits. Toggling perforated anvils shows how much more X-ray light gets through.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why 'smaller beam = higher pressure', how POLAR extends the pressure range about tenfold, and why hard X-rays are needed to see through diamond.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: P = F/A, so the reachable P rises steeply as culet diameter falls. Perforated anvils need ~2× smaller culets for the same pressure (r4). 3–4 Mbar requires ~1 µm beams (r4); the PDR (2017) treats 6–7 Mbar as the practical limit of static compression (r4); double-stage cells have claimed higher (~1 TPa, Dubrovinskaia et al. 2016, cited in r12), but on tiny samples and with debated pressure calibration. Transmission T = exp(−μL): a 100 µm diamond attenuates soft X-rays enormously (r15 quotes >10^12 for 0.5–1.5 keV; NIST data give ~5×10^10 at 1.5 keV and ~10^34 at 1 keV), while a 1 mm diamond attenuates Fe K-edge (7.1 keV) X-rays only ~10× (r15, r46). Partially perforated anvils leave ~0.1–0.2 mm of diamond (r15). Pressure is read with ruby (<100 GPa) or the diamond Raman edge (>100 GPa) (r12).

interactiveIdeas.title: Edge finder: which elements can POLAR 'talk' to?
interactiveIdeas.concept: An interactive periodic table. Clicking an element shows its K, L or M edges inside 2.7–27 keV and which polarization tool works there: phase plates at 2.7–14 keV; no circular polarization above ~14 keV until a polarizing undulator such as SCAPE arrives (and then elliptical, Pc ~75–90%, in the higher harmonics); the SiC crystals near 2.8 keV. It highlights the rare-earth L3 edges (5.5–9.2 keV; L2 up to 10.3 keV), 5d L3 edges (9.6–11.9 keV; L2 up to 13.7 keV), actinide M4,5 edges (3.3–4 keV) and actinide L2,3 edges (16.3–22.3 keV).
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Resonant X-ray techniques are element-specific; the energy window determines which science is possible.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Use tabulated edges (X-ray Data Booklet, r36), e.g. Ru L3 2.838, Pd L3 3.173, U M4 3.728, Ce L3 5.723, Gd L3 7.243, Yb L3 8.944, Ir L3 11.215, Pt L3 11.564, U L3 17.166, Pu L3 18.057, Ru K 22.117 keV. Undulator: E1 [keV] = 0.950·E²[GeV]/(λu[cm]·(1 + K²/2)) gives ≈ 2.57 keV at K = 2.62 (the ID table lists 2.56 keV), λu = 3 cm, 6 GeV. Higher energies come from odd harmonics.

interactiveIdeas.title: The 45-degree trap: why POLAR needs silicon carbide crystals
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors rotate a monochromator crystal. A polarization-factor meter shows the π (in-plane) component reflected falling to zero as the Bragg angle passes 45° (Si(111) at ~2.8 keV). Swapping to 6H-SiC(0006) moves the angle to 61.4° and the light survives.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Crystals act as polarizers near 45°, a key design constraint for measuring 4d metals (Ru, Rh, Pd) with polarized light.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Kinematic polarization factor: σ → 1, π → |cos2θB|. Dynamical π Darwin width scales with |cos2θB|. Si(111) d = 3.1356 Å gives θB = 45° at 2.796 keV. 6H-SiC(0006) d = 2.522 Å gives θB = 61.4° at 2.8 keV. SiC(0006) Darwin width ~0.29 eV, peak reflectivity ~74% at 2.8 keV (r4, r5, r12). This matters for source-generated L-V or circular light. For phase-plate polarization, which is generated after the mono, it matters only through the vertical DCM keeping the source's linear-H as σ.

interactiveIdeas.title: Lens-less magnetic camera: dichroic ptychography
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors scan a coherent spot across a hidden pattern of magnetic domains. Each position gives a speckle pattern; pressing 'reconstruct' runs a toy iterative algorithm. Images taken with left and right helicity are subtracted to reveal the domains. A coherence slider (old APS vs APS-U) shows the reconstruction failing without coherence.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why coherence (laser-like light) from APS-U enables imaging finer than the beam itself, and how circular dichroism adds magnetic contrast.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Overlap ≥60% between scan positions. Resolution ≈ λ·z/(N·p), limited by detector NA and dose, not beam size. Coherent fraction per plane ≈ (λ/4π)/(Σ·Σ'). APS-U gives ~200× gain at 10 keV (r13). POLAR coherent flux is 1.6×10^12 ph/s in 200 nm (r5). The magnetic contrast is the difference of complex transmission for ±helicity; for 3D vector tomography, at least two rotation axes are needed (r32).

interactiveIdeas.title: Polarization switching race
interactiveIdeas.concept: A timeline game comparing ways to flip X-ray helicity: the 2002-era soft-x-ray CPU (~5 minutes), diamond phase plates on a piezo (~13–40 Hz), SCAPE orbit bumps (≥10 Hz planned) and the X-undulator (1–5 Hz). Visitors see how slow switching lets drifts masquerade as magnetic signals.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Measurement design: modulate the thing you want to measure faster than everything that drifts.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: CPU ~5 min helicity switch in 2002 (r29). Phase plates 12.7–15 Hz typical (r15, r12), up to 40 Hz reported (r29). SCAPE orbit-bump scheme: ~30 µrad bumps, ≥95% polarization purity, 10 Hz design (r4, r12). X-undulator: 7.5 mm quarter-period motion at 1 Hz, or 5 Hz with dual-XU detuning (r10).

funFacts: Before the upgrade, POLAR's predecessor 4-ID-D was described as the only hard-x-ray XMCD beamline in the US and was oversubscribed 3–4× (r4).
POLAR flips the 'handedness' of its X-rays by wiggling a thin diamond with a piezo actuator: about 15 times per second today (r12), and 12.7 Hz in the 2007 high-pressure instrument (r15).
In 2002, switching the helicity of sector 4's soft-x-ray circularly polarizing undulator took about 5 minutes (r29).

Diamond is nearly transparent to POLAR's hard X-rays: 1 mm of diamond dims the beam only ~10× at the iron edge (7.1 keV), while just 0.1 mm stops soft X-rays almost completely (by ~10^11 at 1.5 keV and ~10^34 at 1 keV) (r15, r46).
The 9-1-1 T magnet is deliberately cooled with liquid helium instead of a cryogen-free cryocooler, because a cryocooler's vibrations would blur a 300 nm beam (r5).
POLAR's goal pressure, ~6 Mbar, is about 1.6 times the pressure at the centre of the Earth (~3.6 Mbar) (r12, r37).

A wobble of just 0.1 microradian in the X-ray source shifts the monochromator energy by ~3 meV at 8 keV, enough to fake a magnetic signal if the polarization is not switched at every energy point (r4).

The two undulators together would radiate about 20.6 kW at their 9.0 mm design minimum gap, close to the 21 kW limit of the high-heat-load front end; users are limited to gaps of ≥9.1–9.4 mm (r8, r2).
POLAR's hutches were renamed twice during design. The experiments moved from '4-ID-B/4-ID-D' (2017) to '4-ID-B/4-ID-G' (2019) to the built '4-ID-G/4-ID-H' (r4, r1, r12).
POLAR was selected for the APS-U scope in July 2016, after a proposal by a team of 15 scientists from US universities and national labs (r12, r30).
The first scientists to use POLAR, in the January–May 2025 run, came from the University of Wisconsin to study flexomagnetism, which is magnetism created by bending (r19).
Planned ptychography detector distances reach 10 m, longer than the 4-ID-G hutch itself (r13).
XMCD was first observed in 1987 at the iron K edge, a hard-x-ray absorption edge of the same kind POLAR uses every day (r40).
POLAR's First Experiments Workshop on 28 June 2023 was the first in the APS-U series of feature-beamline 'first experiments' workshops (r43).

openQuestions: As-built component positions in 4-ID-B/G/H are not published in a table. The diffractometer (67.2 m) and magnet (73.3 m) positions come from the 2021 town-hall slides and plan. Positions of the B-table components (window, polarimeter, XBPM, chopper, KB3) and of KB1 and KB2 are inferred from the FDR order and scaled from the plan drawing (±0.5 m).

The FDR (2019) put the diffractometer at 61.3 m in an enlarged 4-ID-B and the toroids at 48 and 50 m in a new 4-ID-E. The 2021 redesign moved the toroids to 53.7/54.5 m and the instruments into new 4-ID-G/H. We could not confirm that the as-built layout matches the 2021 plan in every detail.

Source upgrade: the FDR planned two in-line SCAPE devices after the project, and the town hall timeline put the replacement around 2026. The Sep 2026 ID table still shows planar APS30#4/#9. A 2023 LDRD funded a permanent-magnet 'X-undulator' for POLAR. Which device (if any) will be installed, and when, is unknown. Both need a small round vacuum chamber instead of the standard 6.3 × 16 mm elliptical APS-U IDVC.
Whether the APS30 devices are refurbished pre-upgrade structures or new is inferred, not stated.
Directions of the lateral beam offsets: HHLM ~4 mm and toroid pair a few mm horizontally (inboard or outboard?); DCM 15.6 mm vertical offset (assumed upward).
Phase-plate details at POLAR (diamond thicknesses, which plates are in pr1/pr2, actual modulation frequency in user mode) are not published. The 15 Hz figure comes from 2021 planning slides.
The status of the 4-ID-B 2 T electromagnet station in user operation is unclear: it is configured in Bluesky but not listed as an endstation in the beamline directory.
Achieved pressure (directory: 3 Mbar) vs the 6 Mbar design goal; magnet field with DAC (directory 8.7 T vs 9 T spec); 9-1-1 bore quoted as 74 mm (VTI, SRI 2022) vs 3 inches (7.5 cm, slides).

Whether dichroic ptychography/tomography is offered in general user mode (the directory lists 'dichroic imaging, 400 nm resolution' and 'dichroic ptychography' as techniques). Where the 4 m and 10 m ptychography detectors physically sit (possibly in 4-ID-H).
Contents and purpose of the legacy mini-hutch 4-ID-MH (50.5–52.8 m), and the hutch ceiling heights (PDR asked for 6 m at the magnet hutch).

Fate of the former soft-x-ray programs: 4-ID-C closed April 2021 (planned), and 4-ID-E (XTIP SX-STM) lost its source when the canted straight was converted. A 2025 APS photo shows soft-x-ray XMCD by the former 4-ID-C scientist at 29-ID, but no official relocation statement was found.
MagXES instrument design, location within POLAR and schedule are unknown.
The identity of the first POLAR user group (UW–Madison, flexomagnetism) is from APS news; linking it to the Kawasaki group's GdAuGe work is our inference.
Is there a dedicated beam stop or shutter at the 4-ID-G/4-ID-H boundary (needed for H access while G runs)? Added here as an inferred component at ~69.8 m.
Are the 6H-SiC(0006) crystals installed in the CINEL DCM and used in 2026? They matter only for source-generated polarization near 2.8 keV.
